name: Biology: Cells and Genetics
author: Recurse
subject: science
description: Cells, energy, DNA, how genes make proteins, cell division, inheritance beyond Mendel and natural selection.

lesson.intro: Every living thing is made of cells, and every cell carries instructions written in DNA. This lesson follows those instructions from the structure of the cell, to how genes are read to build proteins, to how they are copied and passed to offspring, and how they change across generations.
objectives: Compare prokaryotic and eukaryotic cells and say what the main organelles do
Explain how photosynthesis and respiration store and release energy
Write a complementary DNA or mRNA sequence and trace a gene to its protein
Contrast mitosis and meiosis by purpose, number of cells and chromosome count
Predict offspring with Punnett squares, including codominant and sex-linked traits, and explain natural selection

sections.title: Cells: the units of life
sections.body:
Cell theory has three parts:

- All living things are made of one or more cells.
- The cell is the basic unit of structure and function in living things.
- All cells come from pre-existing cells, by cell division.

Cells come in two basic designs. Prokaryotic cells (bacteria and archaea) are small, typically 1 to 5 micrometers across (a micrometer is a thousandth of a millimeter), and have no nucleus: their DNA, usually a single circular chromosome, sits in the cytoplasm. They also lack membrane-bound organelles. Eukaryotic cells (animals, plants, fungi and protists) are usually 10 to 100 micrometers across and keep their DNA inside a nucleus, along with many other membrane-bound organelles.

Key parts of a eukaryotic cell:

- Cell membrane: controls what enters and leaves. Every cell has one.
- Nucleus: holds the DNA.
- Ribosomes: build proteins. Every cell has them, prokaryotes included.
- Mitochondria: carry out aerobic respiration, releasing the energy in food as ATP.
- Endoplasmic reticulum and Golgi apparatus: make, fold, package and ship proteins and lipids.
- Chloroplasts (plants and algae): carry out photosynthesis.
- Cell wall (plants, fungi and most bacteria): a rigid outer layer that supports the cell.

Plant cells have mitochondria as well as chloroplasts. Photosynthesis makes sugar, and mitochondria then break that sugar down to release usable energy, just as they do in animal cells.
sections.tip: Prokaryote means "before the nucleus" and eukaryote means "true nucleus", a handy way to remember which is which.
sections.pitfall: Thinking bacteria lack DNA or ribosomes because they have no nucleus. Their DNA sits in the cytoplasm, and they have ribosomes like every cell.

check.question: Which structure is found in both prokaryotic and eukaryotic cells?
check.explanation: Every cell needs to make proteins, so every cell has ribosomes. The nucleus, mitochondria and Golgi apparatus are membrane-bound organelles, which only eukaryotic cells have.

sections.title: Energy in cells: photosynthesis and respiration
sections.body:
A sprinter's leg muscles and a sunflower's leaves run on the same energy currency, a small molecule called **ATP** (adenosine triphosphate). When a cell needs energy, to contract a muscle, pump ions or build a protein, it breaks a phosphate off ATP. The real question is where the energy to rebuild ATP comes from.

**Photosynthesis**, in the chloroplasts of plants and algae, captures light energy and stores it in sugar:

6CO₂ + 6H₂O + light energy → C₆H₁₂O₆ + 6O₂

The carbon dioxide enters through tiny pores in the leaves, the water comes up from the roots, and oxygen is released as a by-product. The pigment chlorophyll absorbs mostly red and blue light and reflects green, which is why leaves look green. Most of a tree's dry mass comes from carbon dioxide in the air, not from the soil.

**Cellular respiration**, mostly in the mitochondria, runs roughly the other way: it breaks glucose down with oxygen and captures the released energy as ATP:

C₆H₁₂O₆ + 6O₂ → 6CO₂ + 6H₂O + energy (as ATP)

Aerobic respiration yields roughly 30 to 32 ATP per glucose molecule. Plants both photosynthesize and respire; animals only respire, so they get their sugar by eating plants or other animals.

When oxygen runs short, cells fall back on **fermentation** (anaerobic respiration), which yields only 2 ATP per glucose. Hard-working human muscles make lactic acid this way, while yeast makes ethanol and carbon dioxide, which is how bread rises.
sections.code:
Photosynthesis (chloroplasts, needs light)
  6CO₂ + 6H₂O + light  →  C₆H₁₂O₆ + 6O₂

Aerobic respiration (mitochondria, day and night)
  C₆H₁₂O₆ + 6O₂  →  6CO₂ + 6H₂O + about 30 to 32 ATP

Fermentation (no oxygen)
  glucose → lactic acid (muscles) or ethanol + CO₂ (yeast), 2 ATP
sections.pitfall: Thinking plants photosynthesize instead of respiring. Plants respire all the time, day and night, in their mitochondria; photosynthesis only runs in the light.

check.question: Where does most of the dry mass (the wood) of a growing tree come from?
choices: Carbon dioxide taken in from the air
check.explanation: Photosynthesis builds sugar, and from it cellulose and wood, out of carbon dioxide from the air, with hydrogen from water. Soil supplies only small amounts of minerals. Light provides the energy for the reaction, not the matter.

sections.title: DNA: the instruction molecule
sections.body:
DNA (deoxyribonucleic acid) stores genetic information. Its shape is a double helix: two strands wound around each other like a twisted ladder.

Each strand is a chain of nucleotides. A nucleotide has three parts: a sugar (deoxyribose), a phosphate group and a base. Sugars and phosphates alternate to form the sides of the ladder, and the bases point inward and pair up to form the rungs.

There are four bases: adenine (A), thymine (T), guanine (G) and cytosine (C). They pair in only one way:

- A pairs with T, held by two hydrogen bonds.
- G pairs with C, held by three hydrogen bonds.

So the two strands are complementary: if you know one, you know the other. If one strand reads ATTGC, its partner reads TAACG. It also means a DNA molecule always contains equal amounts of A and T, and equal amounts of G and C.

The information is carried by the order of the bases. A gene is a stretch of DNA whose base sequence codes for a product, usually a protein. In humans, most body cells hold 46 chromosomes (23 pairs), which together carry about 20,000 protein-coding genes.

Before a cell divides, it copies its DNA. The two strands separate, and each acts as a template for building a new partner strand. Each new DNA molecule therefore has one old strand and one new one.

The DNA in one human cell, stretched end to end, would be about 2 meters long. It fits inside a nucleus a few micrometers wide by winding around proteins called histones and coiling tightly into chromosomes.
sections.code:
Strand 1:   A  T  T  G  C
            |  |  |  |  |
Strand 2:   T  A  A  C  G

A pairs with T, G pairs with C
sections.tip: The letters made of straight lines, A and T, pair together; the curved letters, G and C, pair together.
sections.pitfall: Pairing the wrong bases. In DNA only A–T and G–C pair; in RNA, A pairs with U instead.

check.question: One DNA strand has the base sequence GATC. What is the sequence of the matching strand, base by base?
check.explanation: Each base pairs with its partner: G with C, A with T, T with A and C with G, giving CTAG. CUAG uses uracil, which belongs in RNA, not DNA.

sections.title: From gene to protein
sections.body:
The central dogma of molecular biology describes how genetic information flows: DNA → RNA → protein. It happens in two steps.

Transcription. In the nucleus, an enzyme called RNA polymerase reads one strand of a gene and builds a matching messenger RNA (mRNA) copy. RNA differs from DNA in three ways: it is single-stranded, its sugar is ribose, and it uses the base uracil (U) instead of thymine (T). So wherever the DNA template has an A, the mRNA gets a U.

Translation. The mRNA travels out of the nucleus to a ribosome in the cytoplasm. The ribosome reads the mRNA three bases at a time; each triplet is called a codon. Transfer RNA (tRNA) molecules bring amino acids, and each tRNA's anticodon pairs with a matching codon. The ribosome links the amino acids into a chain, which folds into a working protein.

- There are 64 possible codons. 61 of them code for the 20 amino acids, so most amino acids have several codons.
- AUG is the start codon, and it also codes for the amino acid methionine.
- UAA, UAG and UGA are stop codons: they end the chain.

Because proteins are built from this code, a change in the DNA sequence, called a mutation, can change a protein. In sickle cell disease, a single base change swaps one amino acid in hemoglobin, which changes the shape of red blood cells.
sections.code:
DNA template:  TAC  GGA  TTT  ACT
mRNA:          AUG  CCU  AAA  UGA
Amino acids:   Met  Pro  Lys  stop
sections.tip: Transcription makes a transcript, an RNA copy. Translation translates from the language of bases into the language of amino acids.
sections.pitfall: Copying the template strand letter for letter. The mRNA is complementary to the template, with U wherever A appears on the template.

check.question: Where in a eukaryotic cell does translation take place?
choices: Inside the nucleus, next to the DNA
check.explanation: Transcription happens in the nucleus, but the mRNA then leaves through pores in the nuclear envelope and is translated at ribosomes, which float in the cytoplasm or sit on the rough endoplasmic reticulum.

sections.title: Cell division: mitosis and meiosis
sections.body:
Cells divide in two different ways, for two different jobs.

Mitosis makes copies. Before dividing, the cell copies all of its DNA. The copies are then pulled apart, one full set to each side, and the cell splits in two. The result is two daughter cells that are genetically identical to the parent and to each other, each with the full number of chromosomes (diploid, 46 in humans). Mitosis is how you grow, heal a cut and replace worn-out cells. Its stages are prophase, metaphase, anaphase and telophase, followed by cytokinesis, when the cytoplasm divides. Bacteria use a simpler process called binary fission.

Meiosis makes sex cells, called gametes: sperm and eggs. After one round of DNA copying, the cell divides twice. The result is four cells, each with half the number of chromosomes (haploid, 23 in humans), and each genetically different. Two things shuffle the genes:

- Crossing over: paired chromosomes swap matching sections.
- Independent assortment: each pair of chromosomes is split between the new cells at random.

At fertilization, a sperm (23 chromosomes) and an egg (23 chromosomes) join to make a cell with 46 again, half from each parent.

In more detail: during **interphase** the cell grows and copies its DNA. In **prophase** the chromosomes condense and become visible. In **metaphase** they line up across the middle of the cell. In **anaphase** the copies are pulled to opposite ends. In **telophase** a new nucleus forms around each set, and in cytokinesis the cell pinches in two (animals) or builds a new wall down the middle (plants). Cancer is mitosis out of control: mutations disable the checks that normally stop a cell from dividing.
sections.code:
Mitosis              Meiosis
Divisions     1                    2
Cells made    2                    4
Chromosomes   46 → 46 (diploid)    46 → 23 (haploid)
Genetically   identical            all different
Used for      growth and repair    sperm and eggs
sections.tip: Meiosis halves the chromosome number so that fertilization can restore it.
sections.pitfall: Mixing up mitosis and meiosis. Mitosis makes 2 identical diploid cells for growth and repair; meiosis makes 4 different haploid gametes.

check.question: Which process produces human sperm and egg cells?
check.explanation: Meiosis produces gametes with half the chromosome number. Mitosis produces identical body cells, binary fission is how bacteria divide, and fertilization is the joining of two gametes, not the way they are made.

sections.title: Inheritance and natural selection
sections.body:
Gregor Mendel's experiments with pea plants in the 1860s showed how traits are inherited.

- Genes come in different versions called alleles. Each individual carries two alleles for each gene, one from each parent.
- A dominant allele, written with a capital letter (P), shows its effect even when only one copy is present. A recessive allele (p) shows its effect only when both copies are recessive.
- The genotype is the pair of alleles (PP, Pp or pp). The phenotype is the trait you can observe. If P gives purple flowers and p gives white, then PP and Pp plants are purple and only pp plants are white.
- Homozygous means two identical alleles (PP or pp); heterozygous means two different ones (Pp).

A Punnett square predicts the offspring of a cross. One parent's two alleles go along the top, the other's down the side, and each box combines one from each. For Pp × Pp the boxes give 1 PP : 2 Pp : 1 pp, so each offspring has a 3 in 4 chance of purple flowers and a 1 in 4 chance of white. These are probabilities for each offspring separately, not guaranteed counts.

Natural selection, described by Charles Darwin and Alfred Russel Wallace, explains how populations change over generations:

- Individuals in a population vary, and much of that variation is inherited.
- More offspring are born than can survive, so they compete for limited resources.
- Individuals whose traits suit their environment survive and reproduce more, passing on their alleles.
- Over many generations, those alleles become more common in the population.

The mutations that create new variation happen at random; they do not appear because an organism needs them. Selection is the non-random part: the environment determines which variants leave more offspring. Individuals do not evolve during their lifetimes; populations evolve over generations.

The evidence for evolution comes from many independent directions: fossils showing gradual change over millions of years, the same bone layout in a human arm, a bat's wing and a whale's flipper, and DNA comparisons. Humans and chimpanzees share about 98 to 99% of their DNA sequence, and the closer two species are in DNA, the more recently they shared an ancestor.
sections.code:
Pp × Pp

         P      p
   P    PP     Pp
   p    Pp     pp

PP : Pp : pp = 1 : 2 : 1
purple : white = 3 : 1
sections.tip: Each box in a Punnett square is one equally likely outcome, so one box out of four is a 25% chance.
sections.pitfall: Thinking organisms evolve because they need to. Mutations arise at random; selection only filters the variation that already exists.

check.question: A heterozygous tall pea plant (Tt) is crossed with a short plant (tt). What fraction of the offspring are expected to be short?
check.explanation: The tt parent can only pass on t. Half the time the Tt parent passes on T, giving a tall Tt plant, and half the time t, giving a short tt plant, so half the offspring are expected to be short. 1/4 is the answer for a Tt × Tt cross, not this one.

sections.title: Beyond Mendel: blood types, sex-linked traits and mutations
sections.body:
Mendel's peas made inheritance look tidy: one gene, two alleles, one of them dominant. Real traits are often messier, and the exceptions are where exam questions live.

**Codominance**: both alleles show up fully. Human ABO blood type is the classic case. The A and B alleles are codominant, and O is recessive to both. So genotype AB gives type AB blood, AA or AO gives type A, BB or BO gives type B, and only OO gives type O. A type A parent and a type B parent can have a child of any of the four types, if both carry O.

**Incomplete dominance**: the heterozygote is a blend. Crossing red and white snapdragons gives pink offspring, and crossing two pinks gives red, pink and white in a 1 : 2 : 1 ratio.

**Sex-linked traits**: humans have two sex chromosomes, XX in females and XY in males, and the X carries many genes that the small Y lacks. A male has only one X, so a single recessive allele on it shows up. That is why red-green color blindness and hemophilia are far more common in males. A son always gets his X from his mother, so a son's color blindness comes through his mother's side.

**Polygenic traits** such as height and skin color are shaped by many genes plus the environment, so they vary smoothly instead of falling into neat categories.

**Mutations** are changes in the DNA sequence. A substitution swaps one base, which may change one amino acid (as in sickle cell disease) or change nothing at all, since most amino acids have several codons. Inserting or deleting a single base shifts the reading frame, so every codon after it is read wrongly, which usually wrecks the protein. Most mutations are neutral or harmful and a few are helpful, and only mutations in gamete-making cells pass to offspring.
sections.code:
Type A parent (AO) × type B parent (BO)

          B      O
   A     AB     AO
   O     BO     OO

AB : A : B : O = 1 : 1 : 1 : 1
sections.pitfall: Assuming every trait has one dominant and one recessive allele. Blood types, flower colors and height show codominance, blending and many genes at once.

check.question: A color-blind man and a woman who carries no color-blindness allele have a son. What is the chance the son is color-blind?
check.explanation: The gene is on the X chromosome. A son gets his Y from his father and his X from his mother, and her X chromosomes carry only normal alleles, so the son cannot be color-blind. The father's X goes only to daughters, who would be carriers.

keyTerms.definition: A cell with no nucleus or membrane-bound organelles, such as a bacterium.
A cell with a nucleus and membrane-bound organelles, as in animals, plants, fungi and protists.
The rule that A pairs with T (or with U in RNA) and G pairs with C.
A sequence of three mRNA bases that codes for one amino acid or a stop signal.
Diploid cells have two sets of chromosomes (46 in humans); haploid cells have one set (23).
One version of a gene, such as the version for purple flowers or the one for white.
The alleles an organism carries, such as Pp. The trait you can observe is the phenotype.
The process by which inherited traits that improve survival and reproduction become more common over generations.
Adenosine triphosphate, the molecule cells use as their immediate energy currency.
Both alleles show their effect fully in a heterozygote, as with the A and B alleles in AB blood.
A trait controlled by a gene on the X chromosome; it shows up more often in males, who have only one X.
A change in the DNA sequence, such as a substitution, insertion or deletion of bases.

summary: All living things are made of cells; prokaryotes lack a nucleus, while eukaryotes have one plus membrane-bound organelles.
Photosynthesis stores light energy in glucose; respiration releases it as ATP, far more with oxygen than without.
DNA's bases pair A with T and G with C, so each strand is a template for the other.
Genes are transcribed into mRNA, which ribosomes translate one codon (three bases) at a time into protein.
Mitosis makes two identical diploid cells; meiosis makes four genetically different haploid gametes.
Dominant alleles mask recessive ones, though codominance, sex linkage and many-gene traits complicate the picture; natural selection makes helpful inherited traits more common over generations.
lesson.feynmanPrompt: Explain to a friend how a sequence of bases in DNA ends up as a working protein, and why two purple-flowered pea plants can produce a plant with white flowers.

questions.question: Which of these is one of the three parts of cell theory?
choices: All cells come from pre-existing cells
Cells can form from non-living matter
Only animals and plants are made of cells
questions.explanation: Cell theory says that all living things are made of cells, that the cell is the basic unit of life, and that new cells come only from existing cells. The claim that all cells have a nucleus is false: bacteria are cells without one.

questions.question: Do plant cells contain mitochondria?
choices: No, chloroplasts do the same job in plants
Only in root cells, which get no light
Yes, plant cells have mitochondria as well as chloroplasts
No, plants get all their energy directly from sunlight
questions.explanation: Chloroplasts capture light energy to make sugar, and mitochondria then break that sugar down to release ATP, so leaf cells need both. Mitochondria are not limited to roots: nearly every plant cell has them, while chloroplasts appear only in cells that get light.

questions.question: A cell has DNA, ribosomes, a cell membrane and a cell wall, but no nucleus. What is it most likely to be?
questions.explanation: Having no nucleus makes it a prokaryote, such as a bacterium. Plant and fungal cells also have cell walls, but they are eukaryotes with a nucleus, and animal cells have no cell wall at all.

questions.question: A sample of DNA is 30% adenine. What percentage of it is guanine?
questions.explanation: Adenine pairs with thymine, so thymine is also 30%, and A + T = 60%. That leaves 40% for G and C, which are always equal, so guanine is 20%. A common mistake is to stop at 40% and forget that it is shared equally between G and C.

questions.question: Which base pairs with adenine in DNA?
questions.explanation: In DNA, adenine always pairs with thymine, and guanine with cytosine. In RNA, uracil takes thymine's place, so there adenine pairs with uracil.

questions.question: What holds the two strands of a DNA double helix together?
choices: Covalent bonds between the phosphate groups
questions.explanation: Paired bases on opposite strands are joined by hydrogen bonds: two for each A–T pair and three for each G–C pair. Each hydrogen bond is weak, which lets the strands unzip for copying and transcription. Strong covalent bonds hold each strand's own sugar–phosphate backbone together, not the two strands to each other.

questions.question: Which base is found in RNA but not in DNA?
questions.explanation: RNA uses uracil (U) where DNA uses thymine (T). Adenine, guanine and cytosine appear in both. Thymine is the reverse case: found in DNA but not in RNA.

questions.question: How many mRNA bases make up one codon?
questions.explanation: Each codon is a triplet of bases. With four bases, triplets give 4 × 4 × 4 = 64 combinations, enough for 20 amino acids plus stop signals. Pairs of bases would give only 16 combinations, too few.

questions.question: A section of a DNA template strand reads TAC. What mRNA codon is made from it, and what does that codon do?
choices: AUG, the start codon, which codes for methionine
TAC, which is a stop codon
questions.explanation: Transcription pairs T with A, A with U and C with G, so TAC becomes AUG. AUG is the start codon and codes for methionine. ATG has the right pairing idea but uses T, which never appears in RNA, and UAC comes from copying the template letter for letter instead of pairing.

questions.question: Describe transcription and translation: where each happens in a eukaryotic cell and what each makes.
questions.answer: Transcription happens in the nucleus: RNA polymerase copies a gene's DNA into messenger RNA. Translation happens at ribosomes in the cytoplasm: the ribosome reads the mRNA one codon at a time while tRNAs bring the matching amino acids, which are joined into a protein.
questions.explanation: Together these steps are the central dogma, DNA → RNA → protein. In prokaryotes, which have no nucleus, both steps happen in the cytoplasm, often at the same time.

questions.question: What does mitosis produce?
choices: Two haploid sperm or egg cells
questions.explanation: Mitosis copies the DNA once and divides once, giving two cells identical to the parent with the full chromosome number. Four genetically different haploid cells is the result of meiosis.

questions.question: Human body cells have 46 chromosomes. How many chromosomes are in a human egg cell?
questions.explanation: Meiosis halves the chromosome number, so gametes have 23. When a sperm (23) fertilizes an egg (23), the new cell has 46 again. If gametes had 46, the number would double every generation.

questions.question: Why are two siblings with the same parents (who are not identical twins) genetically different?
choices: Crossing over and independent assortment in meiosis give each gamete a different mix of alleles
Mitosis introduces random changes into every body cell
Each child inherits all of its genes from just one parent
Genes are rewritten to suit the child's environment after birth
questions.explanation: Meiosis shuffles each parent's alleles, so every sperm and egg carries a different combination. With 23 chromosome pairs, independent assortment alone allows over 8 million combinations per parent, before crossing over adds more. Mitosis copies DNA faithfully and is not the source of this variation.

questions.question: Two heterozygous purple-flowered plants (Pp × Pp) are crossed. What percentage of the offspring are expected to have white flowers (pp)?
questions.explanation: A Punnett square for Pp × Pp has four equally likely boxes: PP, Pp, Pp and pp. Only pp is white, so the chance is 1 in 4, or 25%. The other 75% carry at least one dominant P allele and are purple.

questions.question: Two parents are both carriers (Aa) of a recessive condition. Their first child has the condition (aa). What is the chance that their second child will have it?
choices: 0%, because the 1 in 4 has already happened
100%, because it now runs in the family
50%, because it has appeared once already
25%, the same as for the first child
questions.explanation: Each child is a separate, independent event, so the chance stays 1 in 4 every time. A Punnett square gives the probability for each offspring, not a fixed quota that gets used up.

questions.question: Many bacteria are now resistant to common antibiotics. Which explanation matches natural selection?
choices: Bacteria chose to become resistant after being exposed
Bacteria that already carried resistance survived treatment and multiplied
Each bacterium gradually learned to tolerate the drug
Antibiotics have slowly become weaker over the years
questions.explanation: Resistance alleles arise by random mutation, often before the drug is ever used. The antibiotic kills susceptible bacteria and leaves the resistant ones to reproduce, so resistance becomes more common in the population. No individual bacterium chooses or learns resistance.

questions.question: What conditions must be met for natural selection to happen?
questions.answer: Individuals must vary in a trait, the variation must be inherited, more offspring must be produced than can survive, and the trait must affect survival or reproduction. Then the helpful alleles become more common over generations.
questions.explanation: A trait that is not inherited, such as a scar, cannot be selected however useful it is. Selection acts on individuals, but it is the population that changes, not any individual during its lifetime.

questions.question: Match each cell part to its job.

pairs.right: Releases energy from food as ATP

questions.explanation: Each organelle has a specialty. Only the nucleus, mitochondria, chloroplasts and Golgi are membrane-bound organelles found in eukaryotes; ribosomes and the cell membrane are in every cell.

questions.question: Put the stages of cell division by mitosis in order.
items: Metaphase: chromosomes line up in the middle
Anaphase: the copies are pulled to opposite ends
Cytokinesis: the cell splits in two
questions.explanation: The DNA must be copied before anything is separated, the chromosomes line up before being pulled apart, and the cytoplasm divides last. A common memory aid for the four phases is PMAT.

questions.question: Put the steps from gene to protein in order, for a eukaryotic cell.
items: RNA polymerase transcribes the gene into mRNA in the nucleus
A ribosome reads the mRNA one codon at a time
tRNAs bring the matching amino acids
The amino acid chain folds into a working protein
questions.explanation: Transcription comes first, in the nucleus; translation happens at the ribosome, with tRNAs delivering amino acids codon by codon. Folding gives the finished chain its working shape.

questions.question: Which gas do plants take in from the air for photosynthesis? Give its name or formula.
questions.explanation: Photosynthesis combines carbon dioxide and water, using light energy, to make glucose and release oxygen. Oxygen is the gas plants give off, which is the usual mix-up.

questions.question: Which statement about cellular respiration is true?
choices: Only animals respire; plants photosynthesize instead
Respiration happens mainly in the chloroplasts
Aerobic respiration makes far more ATP per glucose than fermentation does
Respiration turns carbon dioxide into glucose
questions.explanation: With oxygen, mitochondria extract roughly 30 to 32 ATP per glucose, against 2 from fermentation. Plants respire too, respiration happens in the mitochondria, and turning CO₂ into glucose is photosynthesis.

questions.question: One parent has blood type AB and the other has type O. Which blood types are possible for their children?
questions.explanation: The AB parent passes on A or B, and the OO parent can only pass on O. Children are AO (type A) or BO (type B). No child can be AB, which needs both A and B, or O, which needs two O alleles.

questions.question: Which mutation is most likely to destroy a protein's function?
choices: A substitution that turns a codon into another codon for the same amino acid
A substitution in the codon just before the stop codon
Deleting a single base near the start of the gene
A substitution that swaps one amino acid for a very similar one
questions.explanation: Deleting one base shifts the reading frame, so every codon after it is misread and the protein comes out garbled, often cut short by an early stop codon. Substitutions change at most one amino acid, and a silent one changes none.

questions.question: Select every structure that a typical bacterium has.
questions.explanation: Bacteria are prokaryotes: they have a membrane, ribosomes, DNA in the cytoplasm and, in most species, a cell wall. They lack a nucleus and membrane-bound organelles such as mitochondria.

questions.question: A DNA template strand reads TAC GGC ATT. Write the mRNA it codes for.
questions.explanation: Pair each template base: T→A, A→U, C→G, G→C. TAC becomes AUG (start), GGC becomes CCG (proline) and ATT becomes UAA (stop). Writing T in the mRNA is the giveaway mistake, since RNA uses U.

questions.question: Which pair of sex chromosomes does a typical human male have? Write it as two letters.
questions.explanation: Males are typically XY and females XX. Because males have one X, a recessive allele on it is not masked, which is why X-linked conditions such as hemophilia are more common in males.

questions.question: A woman carries a hemophilia allele on one of her X chromosomes. Her husband does not have hemophilia. What is the chance that any one of their sons has hemophilia?
questions.explanation: A son gets his X from his mother, and she passes on the affected X half the time, so each son has a 50% chance. 25% is the chance for a child of unknown sex, since daughters get a normal X from their father.

questions.question: In snapdragons, red crossed with white gives pink. Two pink snapdragons are crossed. What offspring are expected?
questions.explanation: With incomplete dominance the heterozygote is pink. Pink × pink is like Rr × Rr: 1 RR (red) : 2 Rr (pink) : 1 rr (white). 3 : 1 is the pattern for complete dominance.
